issue: Does a state resentencing that leaves an original conviction undisturbed create a new 'judgment' under AEDPA, so that the prisoner may raise new challenges to that conviction in a habeas petition without it being treated as second or successive?

sides.position: A resentencing creates a new judgment only for the amended count or sentence. It does not reopen an undisturbed conviction, so later challenges to that conviction are second or successive.
cases: Suggs v. United States, 705 F.3d 279 (7th Cir. 2013)
Burks v. Raemisch, 680 F. App'x 686 (10th Cir. 2017)

sides.position: A resentencing that legally invalidates or alters the sentence creates a new judgment that permits renewed challenges to the conviction. The imposition of a new sentence is not the test.
cases: Buenrostro v. United States, 895 F.3d 1160 (9th Cir. 2018)
Donovan v. Massachusetts Parole Board, No. 23-1810 (1st Cir. 2025)

this_court: The majority adopts the position that a resentencing can create a new judgment permitting renewed challenges to the conviction. The dissent says the majority discounted Suggs and Burks, which places the majority on the other side of the split.
quote: The majority is simply wrong to discount Suggs and Burks for relying on pre-Magwood circuit precedent; those courts did so precisely because Magwood declined to resolve the issue.
cite: Donovan v. Massachusetts Parole Board, No. 23-1810 (1st Cir. 2025)
